extracted.intended_audience: students, legislators, policymakers, and general readers of political philosophy and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles for when society or the State may legitimately interfere with individual conduct, with application to trade, police powers, contracts, family, and education. Geared to normative evaluation of regulation vs individual liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual sovereignty over self-regarding actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual is not accountable to society for his actions, in so far as these concern the interests of no person but himself; advice, instruction, persuasion, and avoidance by other people are the only justifiable measures of social dislike or disapprobation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle is stated as a maxim: do not punish or legally interfere with conduct that affects only the agent. Examples: private pursuits that harm only the actor. Anti-pattern: treating all harmful-seeming conduct as legitimate grounds for legal penalty when no third-party interests are implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability for actions prejudicial to others
rubrics_metrics.description: For actions which are prejudicial to the interests of others, the individual is accountable, and may be subjected either to social or to legal punishment if society deems it requisite for its protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the complementary maxim: interference is justified when conduct harms others. Guidance: distinguish genuine harm to others from mere consequences of legitimate competition. Use social or legal sanctions as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm-result alone does not always justify interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Damage, or probability of damage, to the interests of others can alone justify interference only in certain circumstances; many legitimate pursuits necessarily cause loss or disappointment to others (e.g., competition), and society admits no right in the disappointed to immunity from such suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervene only when the means employed to succeed are contrary to general interest (fraud, treachery, force). Example: success in an overcrowded profession harming competitors is not a ground for interference. Anti-pattern: regulating or prohibiting competitive success simply because it causes others' disappointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade as a social act but regulated by consumer freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever undertakes to sell goods to the public does what affects the interests of others and comes within society's jurisdiction; however, cheapness and quality are best provided by leaving producers and sellers free, under the check of buyers' equal freedom to buy elsewhere (doctrine of Free Trade).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations that undermine buyer choice are more problematic. Legitimate regulation includes prevention of fraud/adulteration, sanitary and workplace protections. Anti-pattern: price-fixing or production restraints that do not achieve their intended results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interferences that restrict buyer access infringe liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Interferences intended to make it impossible or difficult to obtain a particular commodity (e.g., prohibition of opium importation, Maine Law) are objectionable because they infringe the liberty of the buyer, not just the producer or seller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess regulation by its effect on consumers' access. Example: prohibiting sale altogether is different in kind from regulating quality or labeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police preventive function must be narrowly applied
rubrics_metrics.description: Government may take precautions against crime before it is committed, but the preventive function is far more liable to be abused than punitive measures; one may interfere to prevent an evidently imminent crime, but where there is only danger (not certainty) the individual's judgment should prevail unless incapacitated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervene (seize/turn back) only when there is immediate and certain danger (e.g., person about to cross an unsafe bridge and cannot be warned). Otherwise, warn rather than coerce unless the person is a child, delirious, or incapable of reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer traceability/evidence regulation over blanket prohibitions for harmful instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Where items have legitimate uses but can be misused for crime (e.g., poisons), prefer regulations that create 'preappointed evidence' — labelling, registers, recording buyer identity/purpose, requiring a third person in absence of prescription — rather than universal prohibitions that impede legitimate use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: require labelling, record time/name/address/quantity/purpose for sales; require third person presence when no prescription. Anti-pattern: blanket requirement of medical certificates that make legitimate acquisition impossible or always expensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted legal restrictions for individuals with demonstrated dangerous conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct such as drunkenness is generally not fit for legislative interference, but a person previously convicted of violent acts while drunk may legitimately be placed under special legal restriction (penalty for subsequent drunkenness and increased penalty for further offences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify personal restrictions where there is a demonstrated risk to others from that individual's behavior. Anti-pattern: applying the same restrictions to all drinkers irrespective of demonstrated harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsion justified to enforce legal duties to others (e.g., support obligations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Idleness cannot without tyranny be the subject of legal punishment except where the person receives public support or when it constitutes breach of contract; if from idleness or avoidable cause a man fails to perform legal duties to others (e.g., support his children), it is not tyranny to compel fulfillment by compulsory labour if no other means exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish private failings from breaches that injure others. Compulsion is acceptable to secure others' rights or welfare when voluntary remedies fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity can convert self-regarding acts into offences against others
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts directly injurious only to the agent ought not to be legally interdicted, but if done publicly they violate good manners and come within offences against others and may therefore be prohibited (e.g., offences against decency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether publicity of an act imposes burdens or affronts on others that justify regulation. Anti-pattern: banning private conduct solely because it is distasteful when not public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice and persuasion are generally permissible social acts
rubrics_metrics.description: If people must be allowed to act as they please in matters concerning only themselves, they must equally be free to consult and advise; whatever it is permitted to do, it must be permitted to advise to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow free exchange of opinions and advice. Caveat: when the instigator derives personal pecuniary benefit and promotes what the State deems an evil, restrictions may be considered because of interest-conflicted promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of interested instigators who profit from promoting harmful conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: When instigators make it their occupation for subsistence or pecuniary gain to promote conduct the State regards as evil, a new element arises (classes with interests opposed to public weal) and society may be justified in excluding solicitations that are not disinterested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prohibition of public gambling-houses or punishment of procurers (pimps) while tolerating private gambling. Anti-pattern: treating private counsel and commercial solicitation identically without regard to conflict of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: State may impose restrictions and guarantees on sellers who profit from abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest of dealers in promoting intemperance is a real evil and justifies the State in imposing restrictions and requiring guarantees which otherwise would infringe legitimate liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means include licensing, regulation of hours, withdrawal of license for breaches, taxation, and requirements as to respectability of keepers. Anti-pattern: assuming dealers' economic interest alone suffices to prohibit legitimate trade entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use taxation/fiscal policy as permissible indirect restraint up to revenue-optimum
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxation for fiscal purposes is inevitable and will unavoidably impose penalties on use of some consumption items; the State should consider what commodities consumers can best spare and prefer those whose excessive use is positively injurious; taxation of stimulants up to the point which produces largest revenue is admissible and to be approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View indirect fiscal penalties as part of inevitable revenue policy; distinguish taxation aimed solely at revenue from taxation intended as de facto prohibition (which is only justifiable if prohibition itself would be justifiable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing and public-surveillance-based regulation of public resorts and sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Places of public resort require police restraint; confine power of selling certain commodities for on-site consumption to persons of known or vouched-for respectability, regulate opening hours for surveillance, and withdraw licences if the house becomes a rendezvous for preparing offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such regulations are legitimate to protect public order; however, numerical limitation of houses to restrict access is generally unjustified and paternalistic unless society has exhausted educative means and can only govern as if populace were children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts/engagements that violate third-party rights or abrogate essential freedoms are void
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagements which violate rights of third parties (or which, e.g., sell oneself as a slave) are null and void; the principle of liberty does not require allowing a person to alienate his freedom so as to be permanently unfree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While voluntary agreements concerning only those parties should generally be kept, the law properly refuses to enforce contracts that injure third parties or amount to abdication of vital liberties. Consider reliance and third-party consequences when assessing enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal limits and moral obligations in personal relations contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagements involving personal relations or services should not be legally binding beyond a limited duration (Von Humboldt); even when legal freedom to withdraw exists, moral obligations arising from encouraging reliance on one's continued behavior affect the justice of retracting obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance legal enforceability with moral duties to those who have relied; marriage is highlighted as having peculiar features where feelings of both parties matter. Anti-pattern: enforcing personal-service contracts at any cost to reluctant parties without regard to third-party effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: State duty to ensure basic education and protect children from parental abdication
rubrics_metrics.description: The State should require and compel the education, up to a certain standard, of every human being who is its citizen; bringing a child into existence without fair prospect of food and instruction is a moral crime, and if parents do not fulfil their obligation the State ought to see it fulfilled, as far as possible at the parent's charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State enforcement can take forms short of full control of content: require education, assist payment for the poor, and use compulsory education combined with State aid. Anti-pattern: leaving education to parental whim where it results in deprivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State may enforce education but should not monopolize educational content
rubrics_metrics.description: While the State may enforce the duty of obtaining a good education, the objections to State education apply to the State's directing what is taught; general State education is a contrivance for moulding people alike and risks despotism of the mind; if State education exists it should be one among many competing experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design policy to secure compulsory education while preserving diversity of curricula and independence of educational institutions. Where private provision is sufficient, prefer voluntary institutions with State aid rather than State monopoly.
